title: Manna (Exodus 16)
hook: bread from heaven, enough for each day, and a double portion before Shabbat

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's timbrel, the drum the women packed before there was anything to celebrate. Your line was bring the drum. What did you bring along? Day ninety-two.

Open your fridge tonight and look at it the way a desert traveler would. Leftovers in the back you forgot about. Three kinds of mustard. A lot of us stock up, just in case, because tomorrow feels uncertain. A month after the sea, the Israelites are in the wilderness, and the food from Egypt has run out. They complain: back in Egypt we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill. And God answers with a strange promise: bread will fall from the sky every morning. But you can only take enough for today. Today: manna.
screen: `THE FOOD RUNS OUT.` → `BACK IN EGYPT WE ATE OUR FILL.` → `BREAD FROM THE SKY, ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God says: "Behold, I will cause to rain bread from heaven for you." The next morning the dew lifts, and on the ground there's something fine and flaky, like frost. The people look at it and say to each other, man hu? What is it? "For they knew not what it was." And the name sticks. Man, manna, is basically the word what. They ate a question for forty years. The Torah says it was white, like coriander seed, and tasted like wafers made with honey. The rabbis added that it tasted like whatever each person wanted. Now the rules. Each person gathers about an omer, a measure of a day's food. Some gather more, some less, and when they measure it, nobody has too much and nobody has too little. And don't keep any until morning. Some people do anyway, of course, and by morning it's full of worms and stinks. Except for one day. On the sixth day, everyone finds twice as much, and the extra keeps overnight, because on the seventh day nothing falls. That's the first Shabbat the people keep in the Torah, and it comes with a double portion. That's why, to this day, two loaves sit on the Shabbat table, and we'll come back to them. The rabbis saw manna as a daily school of trust. You couldn't hoard it. You had to go out each morning and find that there was enough, again. Moses later puts it this way: people don't live by bread alone. A jar of manna was kept, the story says, for future generations to see.
screen: `MAN HU? WHAT IS IT?` · `EVERYONE HAD ENOUGH.` · `NONE LEFT OVER, EXCEPT FOR SHABBAT.` · `A DAILY SCHOOL OF TRUST.` · then, large: `I WILL CAUSE TO RAIN BREAD FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take only what you need today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you tend to over-gather. Food, clothes, tabs open on your phone, worry about next week. Picture the manna rule: enough for today, and no more. Ask yourself what enough looks like, just for today. Then let the rest go for now, the way you'd set down a bag you've been carrying for no reason. The bell holds the time.
Manna. From man hu, what is it? Bread from heaven, gathered each morning, enough for one day, and double before Shabbat.
Your line: enough for today. Today, at one meal or one store, take just what you need, and notice how it feels to stop there. Day ninety-two.

howItsDone: Jews recall the manna every Shabbat with two loaves of challah on the table, and some say a reading about the manna in daily prayers as a lesson in trust.

fork.setup: you've gathered your manna, and there's a little left over tonight. you're worried about tomorrow. what do you do?
options: keep it for the morning, just in case.
eat what you need and leave none.
fork.reveal: the rule was leave none until morning. those who kept it found worms. only the sixth day's double portion kept, for Shabbat.

original.note: Hebrew: manna. the people's question, man hu, what is it, became its name.

trapdoor: what it means: food for one day at a time, with a double portion for Shabbat, a daily lesson in trust.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 16:15 plays on man hu, what is it; the rabbis said it tasted like whatever each person wished (Yoma 75a).

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 16:4 and 16:15.
'A month after the sea' is an approximation from Exodus 16:1 (the fifteenth day of the second month). Confirm.
'The first Shabbat the people keep in the Torah' — Exodus 16:23–30 is commonly described this way. Confirm.
Daily recitation of the manna passage (Parashat HaMan) is a custom in some communities. Confirm framing in howItsDone.
Manna tasted as each wished: Yoma 75a; confirm.
